analysis.one_liner: Bars states from enforcing farm production standards stricter than federal law on goods sold across state lines.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let farms ignore other states' production standards and sue over them, died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop states and cities from applying their own production standards to farm products sold across state lines whenever those standards go beyond federal law and the law of the state where the food is produced. Anyone affected — including producers, distributors, and trade associations — could sue to strike down such rules and collect damages, and courts would generally be required to block enforcement of the rule while the suit was pending. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large livestock and agricultural producers, along with the trade associations that represent them. They could sell into states with stricter rules — on animal confinement, antibiotics, pesticides, or labeling — without meeting those rules, and could sue states for damages and legal fees when a state tried to enforce its own standard. Backers argued this would also lower costs for interstate farm commerce by ending a patchwork of conflicting state rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large livestock producers and agribusiness trade groups

how_it_helps.text: Lets an agricultural producer ship products into any state without complying with that state's additional production or manufacturing standards, as long as the goods meet federal law and the law of the producing state.

Creates a new federal lawsuit route: anyone affected by a state rule on agricultural products — producers, transporters, distributors, consumers, laborers, trade associations, even governments — can sue to invalidate the rule and seek damages for economic loss, with a 10-year window and the option to sue where the plaintiff does business.

Tilts those lawsuits toward challengers: courts would be required to issue a preliminary injunction blocking the state rule unless the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that it is likely to win and that the injunction would cause it irreparable harm.

analysis.who_pays: Residents and taxpayers of states that set stricter food and farm standards. Their rules — including standards adopted by statewide vote, such as farm animal confinement laws — could be invalidated, and state governments would bear the cost of defending lawsuits and paying damages for up to ten years of 'economic loss.' Consumers in those states would lose standards they chose for themselves.
analysis.who_pays_short: States and voters with stricter food standards

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state and local standards that go beyond federal law — including rules adopted directly by statewide vote, such as animal confinement requirements — meaning residents of stricter states could not enforce standards their own voters chose.

The combination of a private right of action, mandatory preliminary injunctions, and up to ten years of damages would expose state governments to a flood of litigation and give regulators a strong reason not to act, chilling state food-safety, animal-welfare, and labeling rules even when they have a solid legal basis.

Because 'agricultural products' is defined broadly under the Agricultural Marketing Act, the prohibition would reach far beyond livestock — potentially sweeping in state rules on pesticides, genetic engineering, or marketing claims for many farm goods.

Supporters' best-faith argument — that a patchwork of conflicting state standards raises costs for farms selling across state lines — has some force, but courts already police genuinely protectionist state rules case by case under the Commerce Clause; this bill would replace that case-by-case balance with a near-blanket prohibition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Uniformity across state lines is a real concern for interstate farm businesses, and a genuinely protectionist state rule can burden out-of-state producers unfairly. But this bill addresses that with a sledgehammer: it would invalidate not just protectionist rules but any state standard stricter than federal law — including ones a state's voters adopted on purpose — and it arms challengers with automatic injunctions and a decade of potential damages. The costs fall on states and the consumers who wanted those standards; the gains flow to large producers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Roger Marshall introduced the bill on August 5, 2021, with four Republican cosponsors: Senators Grassley, Ernst, Cornyn, and Hyde-Smith.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day.
The committee never held a hearing or markup, and the full Senate never voted on the bill before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States and the voters in them who have adopted stricter farm and food standards — such as animal confinement rules — kept the ability to enforce them. Large livestock producers and trade associations gained nothing, and the bills' sponsors may reintroduce it.

against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors — Marshall plus four cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call exists.

industries.note: The bill would let these producers sell meat and animal products into states with stricter confinement, antibiotic, or handling rules without meeting them, and sue those states for damages. Their gain comes directly at the expense of state standards that consumers and voters in destination states set for themselves.
The bill explicitly gives trade associations standing to sue states over agricultural regulations and seek damages, turning associations into private enforcers against state rules.
Transporters and distributors are named plaintiffs under the private right of action and would benefit from a single, lowest-common-denominator set of production rules across state lines.
Their authority to set standards stricter than federal law for food sold within their borders would be voidable, and they would bear the cost of defending lawsuits and paying damages.
